target_customer: Internet businesses and developers who need to accept online payments, later platforms and enterprises
problem: Accepting card payments online required a merchant account, a gateway contract and clumsy integrations, which took days or weeks for a developer.
business_model: usage-based payments API with a percentage plus fixed fee per transaction, plus add-on products

founders.name: Patrick Collison
previous_startups: Auctomatic (acquired by Live Current Media, March 2008)
founders.background_notes: Irish. Co-founded Auctomatic (acquired by Live Current Media, March 2008) per Wikipedia. Founding year: YC page says 2009, Wikipedia body says 2010. Co-founders per the YC company page: Patrick and John Collison.

founders.name: John Collison
previous_startups: Auctomatic (acquired by Live Current Media, March 2008)
founders.background_notes: Co-founded Shuppa, which merged into Auctomatic (acquired for $5M in March 2008 per Wikipedia).

technical_complexity.rationale: Hard parts were bank and card network integrations, fraud and compliance, and building a clean API on top of legacy rails with a tiny team.

defensibility.rationale: Early copying was feasible but bank relationships, compliance, developer mindshare and integrations compounded over time.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: PayPal bought Braintree in 2013 for $800M but Stripe kept growing and stayed independent.

market_need_then: Developers complained that online payment setup was slow and opaque; e-commerce and SaaS were growing and incumbents had poor developer experience.

branding.name_origin: Started as /dev/payments, which failed on Delaware incorporation rules, so the founders picked a new name; PayDemon was considered. One weak source links Stripe to the card magnetic stripe, unverified.
branding.domain_note: Bought stripe.com from its owner around 2011, price reported as tens of thousands of dollars by one source and undisclosed by another

identity.logo: lowercase or wordmark in a purple-blue palette
identity.visual_style: clean developer-oriented design with polished documentation

branding.brand_signature: Highly regarded API documentation and developer experience
branding.community_and_virality: Developers praised its documentation and the seven-line integration online, spreading adoption by word of mouth.

brand_strength.rationale: Became synonymous with developer-first payments; sources emphasize developer trust, but evidence is mostly secondary blogs.

outcome_analysis: Stripe won by making payment acceptance a few lines of code against slow incumbents while e-commerce and SaaS grew. It raised from top investors early, stayed independent when rival Braintree was bought, and by 2025 and 2026 offered employee tenders at valuations of $91.5B and then $159B instead of going public. Rivals PayPal (TechCrunch 2011-09-30 calls the space dominated by PayPal), Authorize.net and Braintree (bought by PayPal in 2013 for $800M) are recorded here because the sources found are dated 2011 to 2013, years after the 2009 YC batch.
notes: Series A: Bloomberg 2012-02-09 reported $18M at a $100M valuation with Sequoia putting in $17M; Forbes (2022) also calls it an $18M Series A; TechCrunch July 2012 called the earlier round an under-reported $20M Series A, so the amount conflicts; valuation not recorded. Series B and C come from the YC blog and TechCrunch. Seed date conflicts (March vs May 2011); TechCrunch 2011-09-30 confirms $2M without a date, so the date is now 2011-03 (Wikipedia's funding table lists 2011-03-28 and a StartupIntros entry is dated 2011-03; other sources say May 2011) and the stage is seed. Wikipedia infobox says 2009 and the body says 2010; YC page says 2009. Later valuations 2021 $95B, 2023 $50B, tenders 2025 $91.5B and 2026 $159B are secondary or tender events. Founder education is from the Wikipedia articles on each founder; no prior employers are stated in those sources. No competitor source dated near the 2009 batch was found, so competitors are left empty. Audit fix: later rounds added, all stage series_d_plus because outlets label them inconsistently (Series D 2016-11 about 150M per Finextra; 2018-09 245M led by Tiger Global per TechCrunch, called Series E; 2019-01 100M rests on a single database, Seedtable, which labels it Series E while others say Series F; 2019-09 250M called Series G by most outlets and Series F by Seedtable; 2020-04 600M is reported as an extension of the Series G or a separate round, with dates and amounts varying from 600M to 631M; 2021-03 600M at 95B valuation per Global Venturing; 2023-03 more than 6.5B at 50B per Nairametrics, called Series I). Round amounts for 2016-11 differ slightly by source (Nasdaq Private Market lists 141M). Valuation is recorded only for 2021-03. The 2010 YC seed was not found in any source opened, so it is not added.
